name: Jah Hut
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Diffloth 1976, 'Jah-Hut, an Austroasiatic language of Malaysia' (SEALS II / Pacific Linguistics) - no open copy; sealang.net unreachable

new_statements.quote: Jah Hut, like other Mon-Khmer languages, has prefixes and infixes but no suffixes; the end of the word is therefore unaffected by morphophonemic alternations, and usually constitutes the root; it is also the only part of the word to receive stress. [p. 102] ... we can distinguish three types of roots: Simple roots, with only one initial consonant, complex roots, with two initial consonants, and disyllabic roots with an unstressed syllable, the 'Minor', preceding the stressed, final, 'Major' syllable. [p. 103]
new_statements.citation: Diffloth, Gérard. 1976. Jah-Hut: an Austroasiatic language of Malaysia. In Nguyen Dang Liem (ed.), South-east Asian linguistic studies, vol. 2 (Pacific Linguistics C-42), 73-118. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 6 Phonology, 6.1 Root structure, p. 102 (PDF p. 30 = scanned/); second sentence from 6.1.3 Initials, p. 103 (PDF p. 31)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable of the word, which is the root ('major') syllable; everything preceding it (prefixes, infixed material, the 'minor' syllable of disyllabic roots, non-final vowels of Malay loans) is unstressed. Words are monosyllabic, sesquisyllabic or disyllabic and always end in a consonant, so the stressed syllable is always the last one.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Disyllabic roots (native ones like /kabok/ 'monitor lizard', /mako?/ 'pregnant', and Malay loans like /sura?/ 'to sing') have a full unpredictable vowel in the first syllable, but it is still described as unstressed (Diffloth p. 103; Matisoff 2003 p. 12).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root plus prefixes/infixes); statement is part of the root-structure description, not a separate suprasegmentals section. No phrase-level or intonation discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Diffloth's sketch covers Jah Hut generally (right bank of the Pahang river between Jerantut and Temerloh, Krau valley; villages Paya Mendoi, Kyol, Kuala Krau named), based on fieldwork 1966-1973; he reports only minor dialect variation (*ua > /wo/ at Paya Mendoi vs /wa/ elsewhere) and makes no dialect-specific stress claims. Glottolog lists one dialect, Kerdau (kerd1240); Diffloth identifies Skeat & Blagden's 'Kerdau', 'Krau Ket.', 'Krau Tem.' and 'Sak. Guai' vocabularies as Jah Hut proper. The statement applies to jahh1242 as a whole.

sources.citation: Matisoff, James A. 2003. Aslian: Mon-Khmer of the Malay Peninsula. Mon-Khmer Studies 33: 1-58.
sources.note: Survey, sec. 1.1(a): sesquisyllables = minor syllable + fully-stressed major syllable; truly disyllabic words keep an unpredictable non-final vowel 'even if the non-final vowel is unstressed (e.g. monitor lizard... Jah Hut kabok)'. Second-hand for Jah Hut (data from Diffloth 1976c).

sources.citation: Diffloth, Gérard. 1976. Minor-syllable vocalism in Senoic languages. In Jenner, Thompson & Starosta (eds.), Austroasiatic Studies I (Oceanic Linguistics Special Publication 13), 229-247. Honolulu: University Press of Hawaii.
sources.note: Comparative Senoic (Semai, Temiar, Jah Hut) paper on minor (pre-root) syllables: 'In all forms of Senoic, the vowel of a major syllable beginning with /h/ or /?/ is anticipated as a minor vowel. That is, a short, unaccented vowel...' (PDF p. 4). Minor vowels are unaccented; major (final) syllable carries the accent. Jah Hut examples given (PDF p. ~7). Supplementary only.
